Abstract 
 
High-performance computing (HPC) systems generate massive amounts of job submission 
logs that provide valuable insights into user behavior and system utilization. However, many 
logs lack critical metadata such as application names, making it difficult to profile workloads 
and optimize resource management. In our five-year dataset collected from the Nurion 
supercomputer at KISTI, more than 32% of 11 million job records were missing application 
information. To address this issue, we propose a deep neural network (DNN)-based 
classification model that can automatically classify application names from job submission-
related metadata. First, we created a labeled dataset with the remaining 78% of data including 
application names and extracted key features for learning. Since the data ranges of each feature 
are different, we applied various preprocessing phases – data scaling techniques to evaluate 
their effects on model performance. Through this study, we confirmed that the model accuracy 
was significantly improved by applying an appropriate scaling method. In particular, when the 
PowerTransformer scaling was used, the F1-score increased from 0.16 to 0.84 compared to 
when the scaling method was not applied, showing an almost 5-fold performance improvement. 
In addition, ablation studies revealed a trade-off between overall accuracy and fairness when 
identity-like features were included, while calibration analysis using learning temperature 
scaling showed that certain scaling methods led to almost perfect calibration with reduced 
expected calibration error (ECE) and Brier scores. The proposed model helps analyze user 
behavior patterns in HPC systems, serving as the first step for smarter job classification and 
real-time system tracking. In the future, this model is expected to improve system efficiency 
by intelligently allocating and managing resources using AI in HPC systems. 
 
 
Keywords: Neural Network, Classification, Supercomputer Log, Data Scaling, Data 
Analysis

1. Introduction  
Supercomputing (also referred to as HPC) systems are essential for supporting large-scale 
computations in various fields such as scientific research, engineering, artificial intelligence, 
and climate modeling [1]. These systems must efficiently manage and process a large number 
of computational jobs submitted by various users [2]. Efficient resource management and 
intelligent job scheduling are essential for achieving optimal performance and system stability 
[3]. The analysis of job submission logs plays a vital role in providing insights into usage 
patterns and improving overall system operation [4].  
Job submission logs typically contain various metadata such as execution time, allocated 
computational resources, and application identifiers. These data help analyze user behavior, 
characterize workload patterns, and understand system-level resource utilization. In this study, 
we analyzed more than 11 million jobs collected from NURION, the fifth-generation 
supercomputer of the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information (KISTI). Since 
building its first supercomputer in 1988, KISTI has continuously advanced the national 
supercomputing infrastructure to support cutting-edge research and large-scale computational 
demands. As shown in Fig. 1, the development of KISTI supercomputers has occurred over 
five generations. Early systems such as the Cray-2S and Cray C90 were designed for vector-
based computation. Later generations integrated massively parallel processing (MPP), 
symmetric multiprocessing (SMP), and cluster architectures, culminating in the introduction 
of NURION, a Cray CS500-based platform, in 2018.  
 
Fig. 1. History of KISTI supercomputers. 
 
Since its introduction in 2018, the NURION system, equipped with 570,020 CPU cores, 
has achieved significant advances in both scale and computational power. As the current 
flagship national supercomputing infrastructure of KISTI, NURION supports a wide range of 
computational science applications across academia, government, and industry. In this study, 
we collected and analyzed job submission logs generated by the PBSPro scheduler running on 
NURION. This dataset was collected over five years of continuous operation and consists of 
more than 11 million job records. This large-scale dataset provides a foundation for developing 
and evaluating AI-based classification models, with a particular focus on classifying and 
analyzing job submission logs lacking application name metadata.  
Recent research has explored a wide range of deep learning applications in HPC and log 
analytics, including service availability monitoring [5], predictive modeling of job 
characteristics [6], and preprocessing techniques to improve classification accuracy [7].

Advanced neural network architectures, such as transformer-based models [8] and hybrid 
temporal frameworks, have demonstrated strong potential in adjacent domains, including 
bioinformatics and system anomaly detection. Despite these advancements, many studies 
remain limited by the absence of large-scale, real-world HPC log datasets, by the failure to 
adequately address incomplete metadata, and by the neglect of feature scaling effects on model 
performance.  
These insights align closely with the outcomes of our study. Unlike prior studies, which 
have primarily focused on forecasting, anomaly detection, or general-purpose classification, 
our work systematically investigates DNN-based application classification in the presence of 
incomplete metadata. By leveraging more than 11 million job submissions and rigorously 
comparing the effects of seven different scaling techniques, our study addresses a notable gap 
in the field and demonstrates substantial improvements in classification performance. 
Building on these foundational studies, our work proposes a DNN-based approach to 
automatically classify application names in job submission logs where this information is 
missing. By training a deep learning model on the portion of the dataset containing labeled 
application names, we aim to accurately infer and fill in missing entries, thereby improving 
the completeness and utility of the logs. One of the core contributions of our work is the 
systematic evaluation of various data scaling methods and their impact on classification 
accuracy.  
Feature scaling is a critical component of the preprocessing pipeline, especially in datasets 
with heterogeneous feature distributions and varying numeric ranges—conditions that are 
common in HPC job metadata. To address this, we evaluate the impact of seven widely 
adopted scaling methods: RobustScaler, Normalizer, MaxAbsScaler, MinMaxScaler, 
StandardScaler, QuantileTransformer, and PowerTransformer. Each method is assessed within 
the context of a DNN trained for multiclass application classification. Experimental results 
reveal substantial differences in classification performance depending on the scaling strategy. 
In particular, PowerTransformer, which applies a nonlinear variance-stabilizing 
transformation to approximate Gaussian distributions, achieved the most significant 
improvement, raising the F1-score from 0.12 without scaling to 0.85. This over sevenfold 
improvement underscores the critical importance of selecting an appropriate preprocessing 
method to enhance model generalization and stability in large-scale, real-world HPC 
environments. 
This paper is structured as follows. Section 2 outlines related work. Section 3 outlines our 
methodology, including data description, data scaling, and neural network design. Section 4 
presents the experimental results, focusing on the comparative performance of different 
scaling methods in terms of classification performance metrics. Finally, Section 5 concludes 
with key findings and discusses future research directions, including real-time log 
classification and the integration of advanced deep learning techniques. Our research 
contributes to more effective analysis and automation in supercomputing environments, 
enabling improved resource utilization and enhanced system intelligence.

Lee et al. [5] (our preliminary research) investigated supercomputing service availability 
using statistical analysis on log-derived metrics, emphasizing operational insights through 
visualization. However, their study did not involve predictive modeling or classification. Hou

Though not focused on system logs, the insight that preprocessing affects model performance 
generalizes to structured data domains like HPC logs. Vasan et al. [8] introduced a deep

classification. 
Hussain et al. [9] surveyed resource allocation strategies in HPC and distributed computing, 
identifying job characterization as a key bottleneck in dynamic scheduling. Our work directly 
addresses this limitation by classifying missing application labels to support workload-aware

developed a deep learning–based system log classifier, but their study neither leveraged large-
scale datasets nor incorporated sophisticated preprocessing strategies. Huang et al. [11] 
introduced LogCTBL, a hybrid CNN–TCN–BiLSTM model for log anomaly detection. While

Although prior research has explored HPC log analysis in areas such as anomaly detection, 
resource scheduling, and general classification tasks, few studies have focused on classifying 
incomplete job logs-especially at scale-using deep learning techniques. Moreover, there is a 
noticeable lack of systematic evaluation on how different data scaling methods influence 
classification performance in such high-volume settings. To address these gaps, our study 
presents and validates a supervised neural network model trained on more than 11 million 
HPC job records. By incorporating various data scaling techniques, we demonstrate that proper 
preprocessing can lead to significant improvements in classification accuracy.  
3. Methodology  
Fig. 2 presents the complete data processing workflow developed for this study, which aims 
to automatically classify application names from HPC job submission logs, particularly those 
entries where the application name field is missing. The proposed pipeline integrates log 
parsing, data preprocessing through feature scaling, supervised learning on labeled dataset, 
and inference on unlabeled entries. Each stage is designed to handle supercomputing data 
while maintaining generalizability and model efficiency.  
 
 
Fig. 2. Overall workflow of data processing.

The labeled dataset is first used in the AI training model, where the deep neural network 
learns how different job features relate to specific application names. After training, the model 
is tested and validated to make sure it performs well on new, unseen data. Next, the trained 
model is applied to the unlabeled dataset-the job logs that are missing application name 
information. The model predicts the most likely application name for each of these entries. 
This process results in a complete and enriched dataset, where all job submissions-both those 
that originally had application names and those that did not-are now fully labeled. These 
improved logs can be used for deeper analysis, such as understanding user workload patterns, 
profiling applications, or improving how the system schedules resources. Because the overall 
workflow is modular, it can be extended in the future to support real-time classification or be 
directly connected to scheduling systems to help manage supercomputing jobs more efficiently.  
This workflow effectively bridges the limitation between raw supercomputing logs and 
actionable, labeled datasets using a combination of parsing, data scaling, and supervised 
learning. This framework lays the groundwork for scalable, automated analysis of HPC job 
metadata.  
3.1 Data Description  
Over a five-year period, we collected a total of 11,395,547 job submission logs (approximately 
1.2GB) generated by the PBSPro scheduler on the Nurion supercomputer. Each log entry 
contains diverse metadata describing the job, including user and group IDs, number of 
requested nodes, wall-clock time, queue type, allocated resources, and-in many cases-the 
application name associated with the job. This rich metadata provides essential context for 
understanding system usage patterns, user behavior, and application-specific resource 
consumption in large-scale HPC environments. 
Upon parsing the raw log data, we discovered that 3,593,664 entries (approximately 32%) 
lacked application name information, a critical attribute for understanding workload 
composition and optimizing resource allocation. As a result, 68% of the logs with valid 
application names were retained to construct a labeled dataset used for model training. This 
subset was cleaned, formatted, and then passed through a data scaling module to normalize 
feature ranges and improve model performance. The labeled dataset thus became the 
foundation for a supervised deep learning classification model.   
The classification model was trained to predict the application name (APPL) using 19 key 
features extracted from each job record. These features were as follows: 'JOBID', 'GID', 'UID', 
'QNAME', 'WAIT', 'RUN', 'CPUS', 'CPU_T', 'MEMKB', 'VMEM', 'STATUS', 'E_CPUS', 
'E_RUN', 'EXIT_CODE', 'SRUTime', 'NODESU', 'MODE', 'WallTime', 'isBB'. Each feature 
contributes specific insights about the job’s configuration, execution, and resource utilization: 
- 
Identification and Ownership: JOBID, UID, GID are used to associate each job with a 
unique identifier and submitting user or group. (To prevent leakage of users’ personal 
information, we trained GID and UID to generate unique numeric identifiers.)  
- 
Scheduling Context: QNAME, WAIT, and WallTime capture how jobs interact with 
the queue system, including their scheduled class and expected execution time. 
- 
Resource Requests and Utilization: CPUS, MEMKB, VMEM, and NODESU provide 
information on how much computational and memory resources the job planned to use. 
- 
Execution Metrics: RUN, CPU_T, E_CPUS, E_RUN, and SRUTime reflect the actual 
performance and consumption during execution. 
- 
Outcome and Mode: STATUS, EXIT_CODE, MODE, and isBB describe whether the 
job succeeded, how it was executed (e.g., batch mode), and whether burst buffer 
storage was utilized.

The feature ‘JOBNAME’ was deliberately excluded from the training process. As this field 
is user-defined, it frequently contains inconsistent, unstructured, or ambiguous content, which 
can introduce noise into the dataset and potentially lead to model overfitting. By omitting this 
field, we ensured that the model was trained solely on system-generated metadata, thereby 
improving robustness and generalizability. The remaining unlabeled dataset-comprising the 
32% of logs without application names-was subjected to the same parsing and feature scaling 
procedures as the labeled data. This consistent preprocessing approach between training and 
inference phases helped maintain distributional alignment, thereby reducing the risk of data 
drift and enhancing model reliability during prediction. As a result, the trained classifier was 
able to accurately infer application names for previously unlabeled records, significantly 
improving the completeness of log metadata and enabling more informed system-level 
analysis and management. 
The classification target in this study is the application name (APPL) field, which indicates 
the scientific or engineering software used for each job submission. During preprocessing, we 
identified and grouped a total of 34 distinct application classes, each mapped to a unique 
numeric label ranging from 0 to 33. Fig. 3 summarized the class distribution across the labeled 
dataset. The two largest classes, etc (label 0) and vasp (label 1), each contain 3,593,664 entries. 
The “etc” class comprises heterogeneous entries that either had ambiguous labels or matched 
predefined heuristic rules without a clear application name. These two classes account for a 
significant portion of the data and reflect both the dominance of vasp as a widely used material 
simulation code and the inherent label noise present in real-world HPC logs.

3.2 Data Scaling  
To evaluate the effect of feature scaling on classification performance and training stability, 
we trained a deep neural network using the selected set of 19 features across eight different 
preprocessing settings: without scaling, RobustScaler, Normalizer, MaxAbsScaler, 
MinMaxScaler, StandardScaler, QuantileTransformer, and PowerTransformer scaling. Each 
configuration was trained for 100 epochs, and the corresponding training and validation 
accuracy and loss curves were recorded and analyzed.  
3.2.1 Accuracy and Loss Trends without Scaling  
To assess the baseline performance of the classification model, we first trained the deep neural 
network using unscaled features over 100 epochs. The model was evaluated using both training 
and validation datasets, and the respective accuracy and loss trends were recorded. The results 
are illustrated in Fig. 4, showing the progression of accuracy and cross-entropy loss over time.  
 
 
Fig. 4. (a) Training and validation accuracy over 100 epochs without any scaling.  
(b) Training and validation loss over 100 epochs without any scaling. 
 
As shown in Fig. 4 (a), training accuracy on the unscaled data starts at about 17% and 
steadily climbs to 49% by epoch 100. This rise demonstrates that the model can pick up useful 
patterns from the training set even without any feature scaling. In contrast, validation accuracy 
exhibits volatile behavior throughout training. Although it initially increases and peaks at 29% 
around epoch 5, it declines sharply thereafter, reaching a low of 5% at epoch 35. It recovers 
intermittently in later epochs (e.g., 23% at epoch 85 and 21% at epoch 90), but fails to show 
sustained improvement. By the final epoch, the validation accuracy remains low at 16%,

underscoring the model’s poor generalization.   
Fig. 4 (b) provides further evidence via the loss curves. The training loss follows an 
expected exponential decay pattern, dropping from 3.2 to 1.5 over 100 epochs. This indicates 
consistent convergence on the training set. In contrast, the validation loss behaves quite 
differently. Starting at 3.4, it remains relatively high and flat throughout training—hovering 
mostly between 3.4 and 3.7, and occasionally spiking above 4.5 (e.g., 4.8 at epoch 95).  
In HPC job logs, fields such as MEMKB, CPU_T, and WallTime can differ by orders of 
magnitude. When these raw features feed directly into the network, large-valued features 
dominate the gradient updates, skewing learning toward those inputs and slowing convergence 
on others. As a result, the model memorizes the training data’s dominant patterns but cannot 
handle the mixed scales in validation, leading to unstable learning and weak performance on 
new examples. These unscaled results establish our baseline. In the following sections, we 
introduce various feature-scaling techniques that normalize these ranges and dramatically 
improve both training stability and validation accuracy.

As shown in Fig. 5 (a), the training accuracy steadily increases from around 10% to 
approximately 67% by the final epoch. This confirms that the model is effectively fitting the 
training data under RobustScaler. The validation accuracy also shows an overall improving 
trend, though with high variance throughout training. While validation accuracy reaches peaks

This behavior is further confirmed by the loss patterns depicted in Fig. 5 (b). The training 
loss decreases smoothly from about 3.1 to 0.5, exhibiting typical convergence behavior. In 
contrast, the validation loss hovers within a broad band ranging from 1.8 to 3.1, with frequent

Compared to the unscaled baseline, RobustScaler clearly contributes to better convergence 
and significantly higher accuracy. However, the large fluctuations in the validation metrics 
point to a need for additional regularization techniques (e.g., dropout, early stopping) or a more 
balanced class sampling strategy to stabilize generalization. In summary, RobustScaler offers 
a moderate improvement in classification performance by controlling feature outlier sensitivity. 
Nevertheless, it does not provide the consistency and stability observed in other methods such 
as PowerTranformer or QuantileTransformer scaling, which are explored in later sections.

This approach scales each input vector so that its Euclidean norm equals 1, thereby 
projecting all samples onto the unit hypersphere in n-dimensional space. Fig. 6 (a) illustrates 
the training and validation accuracy curves over 100 epochs using this normalization method. 
The model starts with an initial training accuracy of approximately 23%, which rises steadily 
to reach around 52%. Notably, the validation accuracy follows a similar increasing trend, 
progressing from roughly 25% to just over 51% by the final epoch. The consistency between 
the training and validation curves suggests a well-generalized model with relatively low 
overfitting.   
Fig. 6 (b) shows the corresponding loss curves. The training loss starts at 2.6 and decreases 
gradually to approximately 1.2, indicating successful learning. The validation loss also follows 
a consistent declining pattern-from around 2.6 to 1.85-without sudden spikes or divergence. 
This stability confirms that Normalizer contributes positively to the training convergence and 
generalization stability of the model. 
Compared to the baseline (without scaling) and more variance-sensitive methods like 
RobustScaler, the Normalizer shows smoother training behavior and improved alignment 
between training and validation performance. While it does not outperform advanced scalers 
such as Power or Quantile in terms of absolute accuracy, it demonstrates reliable convergence 
and robustness, particularly beneficial when the dataset exhibits feature sparsity or directional 
significance. In conclusion, Normalizer scaling provides a balanced trade-off between 
convergence speed and generalization performance, making it a viable choice for scenarios 
where feature magnitudes vary widely, but overall input directions remain meaningful.

As shown in Fig. 7 (a), the model trained with MaxAbs scaling achieved steady 
improvements in both training and validation accuracy. The training accuracy starts at around 
28% and steadily climbs to approximately 58.5% by epoch 100. The validation accuracy 
mirrors this upward trend, beginning near 31% and reaching approximately 56.2%. The close 
alignment between training and validation accuracy throughout the epochs indicates strong 
generalization and minimal overfitting.  
Fig. 7 (b) illustrates the corresponding loss trends. The training loss decreases smoothly 
from approximately 2.1 to 0.5, while the validation loss decreases from about 2.05 to 0.85. 
Importantly, the loss curves exhibit very little fluctuation, and both show a consistent and

4.4 Reliability and Robustness Analysis   
We initially intended to evaluate the model’s robustness to distributional shifts by 
conducting out-of-distribution (OOD) detection experiments using maximum softmax 
probability (MSP) and energy-based scores under temperature scaling. However, the number 
of available OOD candidates—defined as samples with APPL labels not included in the in-
distribution class set—was too small to ensure statistically reliable results. Consequently, 
OOD detection analysis was not included in this study. A more comprehensive assessment 
with sufficiently large and diverse OOD datasets is left as an important direction for future 
work.  
In addition to accuracy, the reliability of confidence scores is crucial for trustworthy model 
deployment. Calibration evaluates how well the predicted probabilities align with the true 
likelihood of correctness. A perfectly calibrated model ensures that, for instance, predictions 
with 80% confidence are indeed correct 80% of the time. We employed temperature scaling, 
a widely used post-hoc calibration method, to improve the reliability of the predicted 
probabilities. A scalar temperature parameter T was optimized on the validation set by 
minimizing negative log-likelihood (NLL). This rescaling smooths the softmax distribution, 
reducing the model’s tendency to be overconfident. 
Calibration performance was assessed using two metrics: 
• Expected Calibration Error (ECE): Measures the weighted average difference between 
accuracy and confidence across bins of predicted probability. Lower values indicate 
better calibration. 
• Brier Score: Represents the mean squared error between predicted probability 
distributions and the one-hot encoded true labels, capturing both accuracy and 
calibration quality.

5. Conclusion  
This study presents a deep learning-based approach for automated classification of application 
names in job submission logs from an HPC environment. Using five years of job log data 
collected from the KISTI-5 supercomputer (NURION), we identified that approximately 32% 
of job entries lacked critical metadata-the application name field-thus impeding workload 
profiling and resource-aware scheduling.  
Our findings demonstrate that feature scaling plays a decisive role in improving model 
performance. For the 1-year dataset, the F1-score increased from 0.08 (without scaling) to 0.68 
when Power or Quantile scaling was applied. A similar pattern was observed in the 5-year 
dataset, where the F1-score rose from 0.16 (unscaled) to 0.84 with Power scaling, representing 
more than a five-fold improvement. These results highlight that appropriate normalization of 
feature distributions is essential for stable learning in high-dimensional, heterogeneous 
workloads. 
Among the scaling methods, PowerTransformer and QuantileTransformer consistently 
outperformed linear alternatives such as MinMax or MaxAbs scaling. Nonlinear 
transformations proved particularly effective in handling skewed and heavy-tailed feature 
distributions, resulting in robust and generalizable improvements. In contrast, simpler methods 
provided only modest gains and were less stable across dataset sizes. Furthermore, dataset size 
was found to significantly amplify the benefits of scaling. Larger training data (5-year dataset) 
not only enhanced classification accuracy but also improved the stability of advanced scaling 
methods. Both Power and Quantile scaling maintained strong performance and adapted well 
to larger datasets.

In summary, this research demonstrates that (i) feature scaling is a prerequisite for high-

scheduling, and intelligent resource management in supercomputing systems. Future research 
will focus on deploying this approach within production-level HPC scheduling systems to 
support intelligent, data-driven resource management.

Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) systems generate massive amounts of job submission logs that provide valuable insights into user behavior and system utilization. However, many logs lack critical metadata such as application names, making it difficult to profile workloads and optimize resource management. In our five-year dataset collected from the Nurion supercomputer at KISTI, more than 32% of 11 million job records were missing application information. To address this issue, we propose a deep neural network (DNN)-based classification model that can automatically classify application names from job submission- related metadata. First, we created a labeled dataset with the remaining 78% of data including application names and extracted key features for learning. Since the data ranges of each feature are different, we applied various preprocessing phases – data scaling techniques to evaluate their effects on model performance. Through this study, we confirmed that the model accuracy was significantly improved by applying an appropriate scaling method. In particular, when the PowerTransformer scaling was used, the F1-score increased from 0.16 to 0.84 compared to when the scaling method was not applied, showing an almost 5-fold performance improvement. In addition, ablation studies revealed a trade-off between overall accuracy and fairness when identity-like features were included, while calibration analysis using learning temperature scaling showed that certain scaling methods led to almost perfect calibration with reduced expected calibration error (ECE) and Brier scores. The proposed model helps analyze user behavior patterns in HPC systems, serving as the first step for smarter job classification and real-time system tracking. In the future, this model is expected to improve system efficiency by intelligently allocating and managing resources using AI in HPC systems.
